title: Herzl
hookLine: Theodor Herzl calls the first Zionist Congress

lines: A NATION STARTED WITH A MEETING.
cards: A man in a black beard and a formal coat stands at the front of a hall in Basel, Switzerland.
In the seats are Jews from many countries: rabbis and students, doctors and businessmen, people who had never been in one room before.
Many came in formal black coats, because he asked them to; he wanted the world to see that this was serious. He wrote plays, and he wrote for a Vienna newspaper.
Now he was trying to win his people a state, starting with a meeting. His name is Theodor Herzl.

teach.b: Herzl had not grown up dreaming of Zion. He was an assimilated Jew in Vienna, writing plays and reporting for a newspaper.
What changed him, by his own telling, was what he saw of hatred against Jews, in Vienna and in France. Even Jews who did everything they were asked were not safe.
So he wrote a short book called The Jewish State.

Its argument was blunt: the hatred would not go away on its own, so Jews needed a homeland of their own, recognized by the nations, and should go about it in the open, with diplomacy, money and organization.
Then he did the organizing himself.
He called the Zionist Congress in Basel, sought meetings with rulers and their ministers, and wrote letters without end. He also wrote a novel about the future land, with a motto on its first page.
In Hebrew it is known as im tirtzu: if you will it, it is no fairy tale. It is a dreamer's line, and also a planner's line.

The psalm about the return to Zion says, "We were like unto them that dream." Herzl's line agrees it's a dream, then insists that wanting it, and working for it, can make it real. Herzl did not live to see a state.

teach.h: IF YOU WILL IT, IT IS NO FAIRY TALE.
teach.b: And not every Jew agreed with him, not by a long way. Tomorrow you'll meet the many kinds of Zionism, and the Jews who opposed all of them. Today, watch one man turn a longing into an agenda.

how: Herzl is remembered in Israel and in Zionist movements as a founder of political Zionism, and his motto, im tirtzu, if you will it, is often quoted; other Jews, then and now, disagreed with his vision.

games.q: you are Herzl. you have written your book, and some readers think you're a dreamer. what do you do next?
o: wait for the idea to spread on its own.
call a congress and start organizing.
games.why: he called the Zionist Congress in Basel and spent his days on meetings, diplomacy and letters.

practice: Let one hope come up that you've long filed under someday: a garden, a language, a call you've been meaning to make. Hold it for a moment as a dream, then ask the planner's question: what is the very first step?
Let the answer be small enough to be real.

wordCard.voice: Herzl. Theodor Herzl, the Vienna journalist who wrote The Jewish State and called the Zionist Congress in Basel. Today's word.
